title: ARIA attributes must be supported by the role
summary: An element uses an ARIA attribute its role does not support, so assistive technology may ignore it. Remove it or use the right one.
problem: An element has an aria-* attribute that is not defined for its role (or its native element). For example, aria-checked is not supported on role="button". Assistive technology may ignore the attribute, so the state you meant to expose never reaches the user.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users rely on ARIA states and properties to know whether something is pressed, expanded or selected. When the attribute is unsupported, they get no state or a wrong one, and cannot tell what a control is doing.
steps: Read the scan result to find the element, its role and the unsupported attribute.
Look up the role in the WAI-ARIA specification and check which states and properties it supports. Every role supports the global ones, such as aria-label.
Swap the attribute for one the role supports. A toggle button uses aria-pressed, a disclosure button uses aria-expanded, and a checkbox uses aria-checked.
If the attribute is the right one, change the role to match instead. If you can, use a native element such as <button> or <input type="checkbox">, which brings the correct semantics with it.

whyItMatters: Custom controls only work for assistive technology users if their states are exposed correctly. A wrong attribute is quietly ignored, so the control looks fine to you and stays confusing to them. This is a WCAG Level A requirement, the level that accessibility regulations and procurement requirements commonly build on.
howToCheck: Re-run the scan. You can also select the element in your browser's accessibility inspector and check that the state you expect is listed for its role.
